headline: Papua New Guinea Communities Sign Historic Forest Protection Agreement
meta_description: 266 clan leaders in Papua New Guinea's Torricelli Mountains signed a legally binding conservation deed protecting rainforest and critically endangered tree kan…
summary_short: After decades of effort, 266 clan leaders across 41 villages in Papua New Guinea signed a landmark conservation deed protecting over 125,000 hectares of forest.
body:
On June 30, 266 clan leaders across 41 villages in Papua New Guinea's Torricelli Mountains gathered to sign a legally binding conservation deed—a relatively little-known legal tool that grants communities the power to protect their own lands. The agreement shields more than 125,000 hectares of rainforest that harbors roughly 4% of the world's biodiversity, including two critically endangered tree kangaroo species found nowhere else on Earth: the tenkile and the weimang. The celebration that followed the signing—dance, song, and jubilation at the Tenkile Conservation Alliance's base in the village of Lumi—marked the culmination of decades of work by the alliance and local communities to fend off logging pressure and secure their forest's future.

The deed bans commercial logging and mining while prohibiting the hunting of threatened species, creating a shield that government protection efforts had repeatedly failed to provide. Since 2005, communities and the alliance had pursued official protected-area status through years of mapping and consultation, but those efforts stalled as government support wavered. In that vacuum, logging pressure mounted, threatening both the forests and the livelihoods of people who depend on them. The conservation deed emerged as an alternative—one that empowers communities themselves rather than relying on top-down government designation.

What makes this moment especially significant is that conservation deeds have already proven their legal worth. A 2025 Papua New Guinea National Court ruling cited one to restrict logging on clan lands in East New Britain, demonstrating that these agreements hold up under judicial scrutiny. The Torricelli deed renews every five years and gives the alliance a model it plans to extend to nearby areas facing similar threats. Since the alliance began working with communities in 2003, tenkile numbers have surged at least threefold, with both kangaroo species expanding into areas where they hadn't been seen in decades—proof that protection works when communities lead the way.
